name: Committed Techniques
description: Build BJJ attacks that preserve useful control when defended by practicing the entry, the likely response, and the position where you intend to recover.
summary: An attack with a fallback gives you a useful next position when the opponent stops the finish.
overview: Commit to the action without assuming that commitment makes it work. Before leaving a strong position, know which connection you need to keep and how you will recover if it is lost.
key_takeaways: Include the failed attempt in your definition of the technique: entry, defense, and recovery belong together.
Identify the control that prevents the opponent from simply leaving when you attack.
Set a point at which you will change plans, such as losing elbow control during an armbar entry.
The same named technique can have a strong or weak fallback depending on your grips and angle.
A planned fallback is a possibility to practice, not a guarantee that you retain position.

bjj_applications.scenario: You enter a mounted armbar and repeatedly end up underneath after the elbow slips free.
bjj_applications.application: Rehearse the entry with a partner who tries to free the elbow. Notice when isolation is lost and practice returning to a top control while it is still available, rather than completing the leg movement by habit.
bjj_applications.outcome: You learn where the attack remains recoverable and where it requires a new decision.

bjj_applications.scenario: You attack a choke from the back and your partner starts sliding their shoulders toward the mat.
bjj_applications.application: Check whether the choking grip is actually progressing. If it is not, use your hands and body connection to recover back control before you lose chest-to-back contact.
bjj_applications.outcome: You can trade an incomplete attack for another chance to control and attack.

bjj_applications.scenario: A sweep attempt is stopped and your partner immediately passes.
bjj_applications.application: Inspect what opened during the attempt. Practice recovering your leg barrier and grips as soon as the sweep stalls, rather than leaving them extended while pulling again.
bjj_applications.outcome: The failed sweep has a rehearsed return to guard.

common_mistakes.mistake: Calling an attack low risk because it begins in a dominant position.
common_mistakes.consequence: The entry itself may release the control that made the position strong.
common_mistakes.correction: Test the opponent’s escape during the entry, not only their defense at the finish.

common_mistakes.mistake: Hanging on to a stopped submission after the controlling connection is gone.
common_mistakes.consequence: You can miss the moment when a recovery was still available.
common_mistakes.correction: Choose a recognizable exit cue and rehearse responding to it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Abandoning every attack at the first resistance.
common_mistakes.consequence: You never learn which obstacles can be solved within the attack.
common_mistakes.correction: Distinguish a remaining defensive grip from the loss of your essential control.

training_exercises.name: Practice the unsuccessful version
training_exercises.description: Choose a familiar attack and agree on one defense with your partner. Begin from the normal entry, let them defend, and work toward your chosen recovery position. Reset when that position is established, the opponent escapes it, or either person taps. Then repeat with the defense unscripted.
training_exercises.focus: Keep an attack connected to what comes after it.

knowledge_assessment.question: What makes a fallback usable?
knowledge_assessment.answer: You can recognize when it is needed, retain the connection it requires, and reach it against the defense you actually encounter.
